name: Konark Sun Temple
tagline: The Colossal Stone Chariot of the Sun God
summary: Designed as a gargantuan 24-wheeled stone chariot drawn by seven horses carrying Surya across the heavens, Konark is the pinnacle of Odishan stone craftsmanship, astronomy, and architectural mathematics.

hotspots.title: Natamandira (Hall of Dance)
hotspots.short_desc: 128 classical dance poses (karanas) from Bharata Muni's Natya Shastra carved in high relief.
hotspots.extended_story: The Natamandira served as a dedicated celestial stage where Maharis (temple dancers) performed Odissi in devotion to the rising sun. Every pillar depicts dancers holding vinas, mridangams, cymbals, and flutes.

hotspots.title: Astronomical Chariot Wheel (Sundial)
hotspots.short_desc: 9.9-foot diameter stone wheel functioning as a high-precision solar clock accurate to 3 minutes.
hotspots.extended_story: Each wheel has 8 major spokes representing the 8 prahars (3-hour periods) of the day and 8 minor spokes. Time is calculated from the shadow cast by the hub onto the intricate bead carvings around the rim.

hotspots.title: Vimana & Gajasimha
hotspots.short_desc: Once standing 229 feet tall, the Deula sanctum was engineered to catch the very first rays of dawn.
hotspots.extended_story: The sanctum was capped by an iron lodestone that balanced the structure along magnetic meridians according to ancient Kalingan Shilpa Shastras.

hotspots.title: Green Chlorite Deities
hotspots.short_desc: Pristine dark chlorite stone sculptures of Surya riding his chariot at morning, noon, and evening.
hotspots.extended_story: Unlike the weathered khondalite sandstone of the main temple walls, the central niche images were carved from dense metamorphic green chlorite imported by sea, retaining their razor-sharp polish for 750 years.

dance.name: Odissi
dance.description: The sculptural curves of Konark's dancers define the quintessential Tribhanga posture of Odissi.

music.description: Evocative of sunset and dusk devotion in Kalinga temple rituals.

audio_narration.title: The Legend of the Sun Chariot

name: Hampi & Vijayanagara
tagline: The City of Victory Carved in Granite
summary: Spanning 4,100 hectares along the rugged granite boulders of the Tungabhadra river, Hampi was the capital of the Vijayanagara Empire—at its height, the second largest medieval city in the world after Beijing.

hotspots.title: Musical Pillars of Vittala
hotspots.short_desc: 56 monolithic granite pillars that resonate at exact musical notes (Sa, Re, Ga, Ma) when gently tapped.
hotspots.extended_story: Carved from single granite masses, the hollowed resonance chambers were tuned to accompany devotional dance without metal instruments.

hotspots.title: Garuda Stone Chariot
hotspots.short_desc: One of only three famous stone chariots in India, housing Garuda the vahana of Vishnu.
hotspots.extended_story: The stone wheels were once freely rotating on stone axles, carved with lotus rosettes.

craft.name: Kinhal Wooden Toys & Sandur Lambani Embroidery

name: Brihadisvara Temple (Thanjavur)
summary: Constructed entirely of granite over 1,000 years ago without binding mortar, featuring a 216-foot vimana topped with an 80-tonne monolithic cupola.

hotspots.title: 80-Tonne Monolithic Kumbam
hotspots.short_desc: Single octagonal granite dome hauled up a 6-kilometer earthen ramp.
hotspots.extended_story: The engineering required elephants and inclined planes spanning from the village of Sarapallam to position the 80,000 kg capstone atop the hollow corbelled tower.

craft.name: Thanjavur Gold Leaf Painting & Bronze Casting

name: Ajanta & Ellora Caves
tagline: Masterpieces of Buddhist, Hindu & Jain Cave Art
summary: Monolithic excavations carved top-down into basalt volcanic cliffs. Ellora's Kailasa Temple is the world's largest single monolithic rock excavation, chiselled downwards from 200,000 tonnes of rock.

hotspots.title: Kailasa Cave 16 Top-Down Excavation
hotspots.short_desc: Carved from top to bottom; zero room for measurement error.
hotspots.extended_story: Commissioned by Rashtrakuta King Krishna I in the 8th century, artisans began at the cliff summit and worked down, removing rock without scaffolding.
